findings.finding: Login brute-force protection has no per-account limiter; the only counter is keyed on client IP + email, so an attacker distributing attempts across IPs gets 5 attempts per source against a single known account
evidence: src/auth.ts:29 — limiterKey = `login:${hashIdentifier(`${await getClientIp()}:${email}`)}`
src/auth.ts:14 — LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT = { limit: 5, windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000 }
src/server/actions/contact.ts:60 — the codebase already uses an IP-independent per-email limiter for the contact form
reproduction: Inspect src/auth.ts:29 — the limiter key includes the client IP
Grep for a second rateLimit() call in the authorize() flow keyed on email alone — there is none
Compare with src/server/actions/contact.ts:60, which does key a limiter on the email alone
findings.expected: A second, IP-independent counter on the account identifier, as the contact form already does — so attempts against one account are capped regardless of source address
findings.actual: A single counter scoped to (IP, email). Each new source address resets the budget to 5 attempts per 15 minutes against the same account
findings.root_cause: The established per-identifier rate-limit pattern used elsewhere in the codebase was not applied to the login path
findings.user_impact: Credential-stuffing or password-spraying against a known admin email is materially cheaper than the 5-per-15-minutes limit implies
findings.recommendation: Add a second rateLimit() call keyed on `login:account:${hashIdentifier(email)}` with a wider window, and fail the attempt if either limiter trips. Keep the existing IP-scoped limiter for per-source throttling
regression_coverage: Mechanical: typecheck PASS, lint PASS, test:unit 19/19 PASS, production build PASS
Still needed: a test asserting both limiters trip independently (requires a database)
findings.fix_applied: src/auth.ts — added LOGIN_ACCOUNT_RATE_LIMIT (20/hour) and a second rateLimit() call keyed on `login:account:${hashIdentifier(email)}`; the attempt fails if either limiter trips. Only the per-IP key is cleared on success, so a correct password cannot reset the budget for an ongoing spray.

findings.finding: getClientIp() trusts the first entry of X-Forwarded-For with no trusted-proxy policy. Re-assessed against the whole limiter inventory: only two of the application's eleven rate limiters are keyed on the IP at all, and both now have an IP-independent companion counter, so a forged header does not reach any authentication or authorization decision. The residual exposure is contact-form flooding by rotating the email address
evidence: src/lib/rate-limit.ts:54 — const forwarded = h.get('x-forwarded-for'); if (forwarded) return forwarded.split(',')[0]!.trim()
src/auth.ts:35 — the login limiter key, the first of only two IP-keyed buckets
src/auth.ts:20 — LOGIN_ACCOUNT_RATE_LIMIT, 20 per hour, added by the QA-AUTH-001 fix this run
src/auth.ts:39 — the second, IP-independent login counter keyed on the email alone, which caps password spraying at 20/hour/account regardless of any forged header
src/server/actions/contact.ts:59 — contact:ip:<hash>, the second and last IP-keyed bucket
src/server/actions/contact.ts:60 — paired with contact:email:<hash>, which an attacker can evade only by rotating email addresses
src/app/api/admin/upload/route.ts:30 — upload:<user.id>: representative of the other nine limiters, all keyed on the authenticated actor id and therefore unaffected by the header

src/lib/env.ts:13 — STORAGE_DRIVER defaults to 'local', and src/lib/storage.ts:10 documents a local filesystem driver, so a self-hosted deployment without a header-normalizing proxy is a supported configuration and not a hypothetical one
reproduction: Grep src for rateLimit( and getClientIp — eleven call sites; nine key on the authenticated actor id, two on the client IP
Read src/auth.ts:35-41 and confirm the login path fails if either the IP-scoped or the account-scoped counter trips
Read src/server/actions/contact.ts:57-60 and confirm the same double-keying for the contact form
Read src/lib/env.ts:13 and confirm the storage driver default is local, so Vercel is not the only supported topology
findings.expected: The IP used for rate limiting is supplied by a trusted proxy and cannot be set by the client, and the supported deployment topologies are written down so that assumption is checkable
findings.actual: The header is read directly with no trusted-proxy configuration. Because every limiter that protects a security decision is keyed on the account or the actor id, a forged header costs an attacker nothing and gains them nothing beyond contact-form volume
findings.root_cause: No trusted-proxy configuration or header allowlist, and no written statement of which topologies are supported — so the safety of reading the header cannot be verified by reading the repository
findings.uncertainty: The prior entry proposed forging the header against each deployed environment. That is the wrong and more expensive experiment: it needs a deployment and a database, and it answers only for the environments tried. The cheap decisive work is a repository-only question that has now been answered — eleven limiters enumerated, nine actor-keyed, two double-keyed — plus one decision that needs no experiment at all: write down the supported topologies. What remains genuinely unknown is only whether a self-hosted deployment exists, which the trust can answer in one sentence
findings.user_impact: No authentication or authorization consequence. An attacker who forges the header can send more contact messages than intended if they also rotate email addresses. The IP component of the login key is effectively decorative, which is worth knowing when reading the limiter code
findings.recommendation: Treat as hardening, not as a live weakness. Document the supported deployment topology in README.md; where the platform offers its own IP accessor, prefer it to parsing the header; if self-hosting is supported, read a fixed position from the right of the chain based on a configured proxy count. Do not spend a deployed-environment test on this
regression_coverage: Proposed: a unit test over getClientIp() with a mocked headers() returning a multi-value chain, asserting which element is selected — no database required
Proposed: assert the login path still refuses after 20 account-scoped attempts when the IP-scoped key is rotated
findings.severity_revision: Medium -> Low, and SUSPECTED -> CONFIRMED. The code behaviour is certain by reading; what was uncertain was the consequence. Enumerating all eleven limiters shows the consequence is small, and the QA-AUTH-001 fix landed this run removed the worst of it. The prior entry's claim that 'every IP-scoped rate limit in the application can be bypassed' is literally true and materially misleading: there are two, and both are double-keyed.

findings.finding: A rate-limited login returns the same null result as an invalid password, so a locked-out user receives 'invalid credentials' with no indication they must wait. Evidence line numbers re-verified: the QA-AUTH-001 fix shifted them, and the condition now covers two limiters
evidence: src/auth.ts:41 — if (!limit.success || !accountLimit.success) return null; (was :31 before the QA-AUTH-001 fix)

src/lib/rate-limit.ts:41 — resetAt is already returned by rateLimit(), so the information needed for the message exists
reproduction: Submit six failed logins for the same account from one address within fifteen minutes
Observe that the sixth response is indistinguishable from the fifth
Read src/auth.ts:41 and :45 and confirm both paths return the same null
findings.expected: The user learns that further attempts are temporarily blocked, with the reset time
findings.actual: An identical generic failure. A legitimate user who mistypes repeatedly believes their password is wrong and may reset it unnecessarily

findings.actual: Two rules on the same data. The most prominent claim on the site asserts registration from a number while the Evidence Center, reading the same profile, reports registration as undocumented
findings.root_cause: The November safeguard was applied to the evidence-coverage query only. The hero predates it, carries its own written rule in a code comment, and was not revisited — so neither author was wrong relative to what they could see

findings.finding: Nothing constrains the unit of figures sharing one metricKey, and the year-on-year chart plots every period of a key on one axis without rendering the unit. Re-assessed: the dropped unit label is confirmed by reading and is a defect on its own; the two-units-under-one-key scenario remains unconfirmed, and the preventive fix costs less than the experiment that would justify it
evidence: src/lib/validations/admin.ts:190 — metricSchema accepts a free metricKey slug and free-text unitEn/unitTa with no cross-field rule
src/app/[locale]/impact/page.tsx:39 — series groups metrics by metricKey alone
src/app/[locale]/impact/page.tsx:88 — the BarChart receives value and a display string built from prefix/suffix; unit is not passed
src/components/impact/bar-chart.tsx:29 — bar lengths are scaled against the maximum value in the group
README.md:27 — 'Figures in different units are never added together'
prisma/schema.prisma:1510 — ImpactMetric.value, the field being charted (see QA-DATA-006 for its numeric type, a separate question)
reproduction: Read src/app/[locale]/impact/page.tsx:39 and confirm metricKey is the only grouping key
Read src/app/[locale]/impact/page.tsx:88 and src/components/impact/bar-chart.tsx:29 and confirm no unit reaches the chart and the scale is shared across the group
Read src/lib/validations/admin.ts:190 and confirm nothing prevents two published figures with one metricKey and different units
findings.expected: Figures are compared on one scale only when they share a unit, and the unit is visible wherever the number is
findings.actual: Confirmed by reading: the chart renders no unit at all, on a transparency site. Unconfirmed: whether any real dataset has one metricKey carrying two units, which is what turns a missing label into a misleading trend
findings.root_cause: metricKey is the only grouping key; the unit is display metadata on the tile and is dropped on the chart path. No cross-field rule ties a key to a unit at write time
findings.uncertainty: The prior entry proposed seeding two figures with one key and different units and rendering /en/impact — a database, a seed and a render. Two cheaper routes exist. (1) The decisive read-only query against real data, one statement, no seeding: SELECT "metricKey", COUNT(DISTINCT "unitEn") FROM "ImpactMetric" WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED' GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT "unitEn") > 1 — it answers both whether it happens and how often, which the seeded render cannot. (2) Cheaper still: add the unit-consistency refine to metricSchema, which makes the question moot. When the preventive fix is smaller than the experiment that would justify it, skip the experiment. No database was authorized for this run, so neither was executed
findings.user_impact: A published figure on a transparency site is rendered with no unit today. If a key ever carries two units, the chart presents unlike quantities as a trend with no label that would let a reader notice
findings.recommendation: Do both halves, in this order. First, pass the unit through to the chart title and table header — this is the confirmed defect and it needs no decision. Second, add a refine to metricSchema rejecting a published figure whose unit differs from other published figures with the same metricKey, or group the series by metricKey plus unit. Run the one-statement query above first only if the refine would need a data migration
regression_coverage: Proposed: a unit-consistency test over published metrics grouped by metricKey
Proposed: assert the chart renders the unit for a single-unit group (fails today)
findings.severity_revision: Severity unchanged at Medium. Re-scoped: the confirmed half is the missing unit label, the speculative half is the multi-unit dataset. The cheapest settling experiment is a one-statement read-only query, not a seeded render — and the preventive fix is cheaper than either.
